title: AfD: The far-right earthquake in Saxony-Anhalt
gist: The AfD took roughly 44% in Saxony-Anhalt — the largest vote share by any party at a German election in a decade, but short of a majority — leaving government formation dependent on either CDU defections from the 'firewall' or toleration by the left-conservative BSW, and setting up a stress test that the author expects to erode Merz's reform agenda and leave Berlin inward-looking and incapable of international initiative.

themes.theme: The 44% result and the arithmetic of power

insights.claim: The AfD won some 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the largest share attained by any party at a German election in the past decade, yet remains just short of a parliamentary majority in a state of only about two million inhabitants.
insights.so_what: A 44% far-right share without a majority is the maximally destabilising outcome — it forces every other party into a visible choice, and that choice is the market-relevant event.
insights.locator: Home to only about two million inhabitants
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: German government formation in Saxony-Anhalt reduces to two paths: CDU members breaking ranks with the firewall to support the AfD, or the left-conservative populist BSW, which unexpectedly won enough seats to form a majority with the AfD, tolerating an AfD government without joining it.
insights.so_what: Watch BSW toleration as the likeliest mechanism — it lets the firewall be breached without any mainstream party formally breaking it, which is the precedent that matters nationally.
insights.locator: In Saxony-Anhalt, the “firewall” leaves two options
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: The next few weeks of coalition negotiation are a stress test for the entire German political system rather than a local constitutional matter, because they establish how mainstream parties handle a radical right that is popular and near power rather than abstract.
insights.so_what: Treat Saxony-Anhalt coalition talks as a leading indicator for German federal politics and for European risk premia, not as regional noise.
insights.quote: No comparable democracy has constructed itself to such a degree upon its capacity to withstand the political extremes.
insights.locator: Though the AfD’s vote share was the largest
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

themes.theme: The firewall as identity, and its cracks

insights.claim: The firewall prohibiting formal cooperation with the AfD is for Friedrich Merz's CDU above all a statement of political identity — norm-abiding centrist conservatism against the extremes — which makes abandoning it costlier than pure coalition arithmetic implies.
insights.so_what: Because the firewall is identity rather than tactics, expect the CDU to absorb governing paralysis rather than break it quickly — which prolongs instability instead of resolving it.
insights.locator: The key term here is the “firewall”
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: The BSW holds the firewall to be a strategic error and has kept open the possibility of talking with the far right on shared issues, making a breakout force from the German far-left the potential prop for a party branch officially labelled right-wing extremist.
insights.so_what: Left-right labels are no longer predictive of coalition behaviour in Germany; model parties by issue overlap (energy, Ukraine, migration) instead.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

themes.theme: Energy and Ukraine as the overlap

insights.claim: The AfD and BSW share concrete policy ground: the BSW rails against Germany's renewable energy push and demands an end to German support for Ukraine, with energy costs and the presence of Ukrainian refugees key themes for both parties.
insights.so_what: A populist bloc aligned against both the Energiewende and Ukraine aid is a direct risk to German renewables policy continuity and to EU defence-support cohesion.
insights.locator: But overlapping policy positions do exist
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: The recent drone attack in Leipzig, for which Berlin has blamed Russia, supplied ammunition for AfD and BSW fearmongering about escalation and German responsibility for the war — showing foreign policy shocks now transmit directly into regional German votes.
insights.so_what: Further hybrid incidents on German soil may boost, not suppress, anti-Ukraine parties — an inverted reaction function worth modelling before the next escalation.
insights.locator: the recent drone attack in Leipzig
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

themes.theme: What a state-level AfD government actually controls

insights.claim: An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would have no say over foreign affairs under Germany's constitution but could shape culture, education, inner security and some fields of migration policy.
insights.so_what: The direct policy risk from a state-level AfD win is narrow; the mispricing risk is assuming it touches federal foreign or fiscal policy.
insights.locator: Should it gain power in Saxony-Anhalt
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: The real value of a government seat in Magdeburg to the AfD is the platform: a loudspeaker to push the national agenda in its own direction rather than substantive state powers.
insights.so_what: Judge the impact by national polling drift after the handover, not by Saxony-Anhalt legislation.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: The AfD has become so ubiquitous that German elections are now framed as binary contests between the populist far right and everyone else, squeezing out discourse on any other terms.
insights.so_what: Binary framing structurally advantages the insurgent by making every election a referendum on it — expect continued vote-share ratchet rather than mean reversion.
insights.quote: They have colonised the minds of the other parties.
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: The same logic is visible in France, where centrist candidates for next year's presidential election already frame themselves as the best alternative to far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen, though Le Pen's 'de-demonisation' strategy contrasts with the AfD's unapologetic radicalisation and she has distanced herself from the German party.
insights.so_what: French and German far-right trajectories share political logic but differ in strategy; Le Pen's mainstreaming makes a French governing outcome more plausible than a German one.
insights.locator: It is a common pattern. In France
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

themes.theme: Merz under pressure and a diminished Berlin

insights.claim: The CDU-SPD government in Berlin has deteriorated through 2026 with policy deadlocks, internal fights and rumours of moves to depose both party leaderships, and Merz responded to the Saxony-Anhalt result by refusing to resign while vaguely promising 'consequences'.
insights.so_what: Leadership risk in Berlin is live; further poor results in eastern state elections are the identified trigger.
insights.quote: What started as a hopeful year of reform has collapsed into a year of despair.
insights.locator: And what of the consequences for Germany itself?
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: Miserable results in other forthcoming eastern German elections could push Merz over the edge, while in the short term the new political reality further erodes both his reform agenda and the firewall itself.
insights.so_what: Discount the delivery odds on German domestic reform and fiscal packages; the political capital to pass them is draining.
insights.locator: In the short term, the new political reality
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla

insights.claim: Other European capitals should brace for a fundamentally changed German political culture and a Berlin government so mired in domestic trouble it is incapable of initiative on the world stage.
insights.so_what: A passive Germany removes the EU's usual convening engine — expect slower European decisions on Ukraine, defence and fiscal integration over the medium term.
insights.quote: a government in Berlin that is ever more mired in its domestic troubles and incapable of initiative on the world stage
insights.locator: And in the medium term, leaders in other European capitals
insights.speaker: Marcus Colla
